title: Contextuality & Cost: workshop takeaways + experiments to try
content:
Quick intro: notes from the small Contextuality & Cost workshop (internal + a few external folks) on 2026-06-22. Intended as a personal scratchpad: distill useful threads, list immediate experiments, and record open questions. Not polished — mostly shorthand and TODOs.

High-level themes that kept coming up:
- Context is expensive along two axes: memory (KV cache size, eviction cost) and compute (per-token attention + cache management).
- Many proposed hacks reduce token cost but shift complexity to engineering (sharding, compression, lossy eviction). Weighing real end-to-end latency/cost is critical.
- Evaluation mismatch: academic papers often report FLOPs or token throughput; product constraints care about p95 latency, tail behavior with mixed sequence lengths, and predictable SLOs.

Useful papers / links discussed (quick notes):
- arXiv:2403.01234 "Sparse KV Compression for Long Context" (internal reading). Key idea: slice attention keys into segments and quantize rarer segments. Promises 3x storage saving with minimal gen quality drop on reasoning tasks. Note: results focus on average perplexity, not hallucination-sensitive metrics.
- Blog: "When Prefix-Caching Breaks" — pragmatic examples of chained prompts causing stale cache hits. Lesson: caching strategies must be aware of prompt semantics and retrieval-based updates.
- Github proto: kv-compression-proto — early code for two compression modes: per-shard PQ and delta-quant. Good starting point for benchmarking on our serving runtime.

Takeaways from discussion (my paraphrase):
1) Baseline instrumentation gaps we need to fill before experimenting:
   - token-level cost trace that attributes tokens to cache hits vs recompute (not just p50/p95 latencies).
   - per-request sequence-length histogram coupled with model variant used.
   - eviction/reconstruction wall-clock costs when using persistent kv stores.
2) Safety/QA: small compression errors can produce large downstream hallucinations on narrow QA tasks. Any lossy compression experiments must include targeted hallucination/regression tests.
3) Routing and fallbacks: cheaper compressed model variant should be able to accept degraded kv format; falling back to a full precision path on confidence thresholds (or eval set triggers) is desirable.

Immediate experiments to run (prioritized):
- EXP-A: microbench compressed PQ shards on a 7B model in dev cluster. Measure disk+RAM savings, per-token latency, and a small QA eval of 120 curated prompts. Hypothesis: PQ reduces mem by ~2.5x, tail latency remains within 1.15x baseline. Owner: Marco. Timebox: 2 weeks. Jira: INF-4217.
- EXP-B: prefix-churn simulation. Create synthetic workload that simulates 30% of requests doing prompt-chaining updates (append-only). Test eviction policies: LRU, TTL-by-session, and semantic-top-K. Metric: percent of stale prefix hits and quality degradation. Owner: Aisha. Timebox: 1 week.
- EXP-C: conservative lossy mode + QA gating. Deploy compressed shards but add an output-level regression probe (exact-match on known queries + heuristic hallucination detector). If probe fails, route to full precision model and log. Owner: Lia. Timebox: 3 weeks.

Instrumentation specifics (implementation notes):
- Add a lightweight token attribution header in runtime traces: {request_id, model_variant, token_count_cached, token_count_generated, cache_hit_ratio}. Start with structured logs to S3 and ship subset to Console.
- Tag requests that hit compressed-kv with 'kv:compressed' label to allow per-route cost breakdown.
- Capture KV rebuild time (ms) when reconstructing evicted keys from persistent store — important for bursty workloads.

Small design sketches / heuristics we mentioned: 
- Probabilistic TTL: for conversational sessions, instead of strict LRU evict oldest rarely-used keys with probability p = alpha * exp(-age/scale). Tunable alpha/scale per-customer.
- Semantic Top-K eviction: keep keys whose embeddings have cosine similarity > theta to the current context embedding. Requires cheap approximate embedding computation on insertion.
- Lossy compression schedule: keep recent 1k tokens at FP16, compress older tokens using PQ or one-bit quantization. Idea: recency-aware fidelity.

Open questions / unknowns to resolve: 
- How sensitive are retrieval-augmented pipelines to subtle kv perturbations? Need a small study on RAG QAs where knowledge references are precise (names, numbers).
- Cost accounting: if compression increases CPU per-token slightly but reduces GPU memory which permits higher batch sizes, how do we model net cost? Need end-to-end cost sim.
- Multi-tenant interaction: compressed shards share memory across customers — does eviction fairness create observable degradations?

Notes from hallway convo with external researcher (M. Chen): they recommended a two-stage eval: synthetic stress tests (edge cases) + closed-book downstream tasks (where hallucination penalty is high). Good note — add to EXP-A/B/C as failure modes.

Action items (short):
- [ ] Lia: draft perf spec for token-level attribution (due 2026-06-29).
- [ ] Marco: spin up EXP-A baseline run (dev cluster) and push initial numbers to the shared spreadsheet.
- [ ] Aisha: synthetic prefix-churn generator + initial policy sweep.
- [ ] Noah: prototype embedding-on-insert microservice feasibility for semantic eviction.

References to attach to shared Confluence page: arXiv paper, github proto, initial spreadsheet for EXP-A (link in linked_artifacts).

Rough ETA to usable signal: 3–5 weeks if all owners run timeboxed experiments. If results are promising, next step is a small pilot on Dedicated capacity for a friendly customer to validate multi-tenant interactions.

Random thoughts / heuristics for future brainstorming (unstructured):
- Could we opportunistically use client-side prompts to indicate which parts of context are "sticky"? e.g., an API flag marking tokens as high-fidelity. Cheap but relies on client discipline.
- For long-running chat sessions, consider periodic snapshotting at semantic boundaries (topic shifts) to compress prior segments more aggressively.

End. This is a working scratchpad — will refine into an internal PRD if experiments show promising tradeoffs.
